content:
The U.S. Department of Justice has successfully paused an order that required it to respond to Apple’s document requests to 14 federal agencies. The DOJ is appealing an ongoing antitrust case against Apple. Details below.

A bit of background

A few weeks ago, special master Judge Jose Linares ruled in favor of Apple in its attempt to seek documents from 14 federal agencies. The case is part of the DOJ’s ongoing antitrust lawsuit against Apple.

In short, Apple is seeking these documents to study how the agencies evaluate privacy and security when crafting smartphone policies and making procurement decisions.

Apple argues that these records could support its argument that some of the practices challenged by the DOJ are legitimate product differentiation and security measures rather than anticompetitive restrictions.

Specifically, Apple is seeking documents from the following agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

After Judge Linares ruled in favor of Apple, the DOJ asked him to reconsider the decision. After Linares denied that request, the DOJ appealed to District Court Judge Julien Neals and asked Linares to pause the document production order while the appeal was considered.

Which brings us to today’s developments.

DOJ gets temporary reprieve

In an earlier ruling, Judge Linares granted the DOJ’s request to pause the document production order while District Judge Neals considers the government’s appeal. The issue on appeal is whether the DOJ must respond to Apple’s document requests.

Judge Linares said that while he agreed with Apple that the DOJ faces "an uphill battle" to win its appeal, that alone was not enough to deny the government’s request to stay the order.

He also agreed with the DOJ’s argument that requiring the 14 agencies to respond to Apple’s document requests would involve "purportedly enormous workloads" and that imposing that burden would be "patently unfair" if Judge Neals ultimately reversed his decision.

Additionally, Judge Linares rejected Apple’s argument that pausing the order while Judge Neals considered whether to reverse the decision would harm the company by further delaying its efforts to obtain the documents. The judge said the case was "still at a fairly early stage of discovery" and that other discovery could continue in the meantime.

With the order now paused, Apple will have an opportunity to respond to the government’s appeal, after which the DOJ will have seven calendar days to file its reply. Judge Neals will then decide whether to uphold or reverse Judge Linares’s original document production order.
